The median home in Park Forest was built in 1958. Across the 9,015 housing units here, 90.2 percent went up before 1980 and 1.8 percent date to 1939 or earlier. That single figure decides more about a paint job than anything else anyone will ask you on the phone.

The tenure split is 5,296 owner households against 2,917 renting, or 64.5 percent owner occupied. Structure follows it: 61.9 percent detached houses, 25.8 percent townhomes and rowhouses, 12.3 percent in buildings of two or more. At 5.8 rooms a unit, that is the trim footage an interior quote is really made of. Median home value is $106,200.

Park Forest is in the top four of the 54 suburbs and towns covered here for the largest townhome and rowhouse share (25.8 percent) and the lowest median home value ($106,200).

Three figures put Park Forest a long way from the average of the 76 places on this site: townhomes and rowhouses at 25.8 percent against a 7.5 percent average, prewar housing at 1.8 percent against a 15.8 percent average and housing in buildings of two or more at 12.3 percent against a 29 percent average.

Source: U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2019-2023 (tables B25003, B25024, B25034, B25035, B25077). Every dollar figure on this page is a published Census estimate of what homes in the area are worth. None of it is a price for work.

What the age of the housing here means for an interior job

Of the 9,015 housing units counted in Park Forest, 90.2 percent went up before 1980. There is no pre-1978 bucket, so 1980 is the nearest line the Census draws for Park Forest. Anything built before 1978 sits inside the federal Renovation, Repair and Painting rule the moment work disturbs its paint. Illinois never took the program on, so the agency behind it here is EPA itself.

What it changes is the front and the back of a Park Forest job, not the middle: plastic and sealed openings before, a specific cleanup standard after. It starts at roughly six square feet of disturbed paint per room inside, twenty square feet outside, and always on window replacement.

None of it is graded at the town line. The rule attaches to a build year and to the work being done, so the number worth checking is the one on your own deed in Park Forest.

None of that is a reason to leave a Park Forest house unpainted. It is a reason to know what the setup looks like before anyone opens a sander, and to hear it from the person doing the work rather than from a website.

Certification is a document, not a sentence on a website. It shows as pending below because no number has been supplied. Ask to see it, in Park Forest and everywhere else.

How the age of the stock changes the work here

A 1958 median build year means plaster as well as drywall, and the two do not take a repair the same way. Plaster cracks along the lath and comes back if it is only filled, so the honest version of a wall repair here is longer than a drywall patch and should read that way on the quote. With 5.8 rooms on the median unit, the trim is the other half of the job. 25.8 percent attached housing means shared walls, shared elevations and often a shared decision. Association work runs to a schedule rather than to weather, and the matching has to be exact rather than close.

What an estimate here has to account for

  • Matching, exactly. 25.8 percent of units are attached, and on a shared elevation close is not good enough. Existing color has to be matched rather than approximated.
  • Distance, stated. Park Forest is 18.9 straight-line miles from the shop. Travel to Park Forest is not a hidden line item on this site and it should not be one on a written quote either.
  • Containment, not just paint. 90.2 percent of housing in Park Forest was built before 1980, so on most addresses here the lead-safe setup and the cleanup are part of the job and part of the hours.

What the housing here is likely made of

Most of it is postwar brick: bungalow, Cape Cod and the first generation of ranch. Little of the outside takes paint at all, so a Park Forest exterior is soffit, fascia, overhangs, doors and the garage. Inside it is small rooms with a great deal of casing in them.

Two figures produce that sentence and no others: build year 1958, and a stock that is 61.9 percent detached, 25.8 percent attached and 12.3 percent in buildings of two or more.

Read it as a starting assumption rather than a finding. No public dataset records what the walls in Park Forest are made from, so attaching a number to it would mean inventing one. The house itself answers faster than any table can.

Questions

Asked about Park Forest

What changes the price most on a house here?

Condition, not size. On 1958-median stock in Park Forest what varies is how much has to come off or be made good before anything goes on: loose paint, failed caulk, damaged trim, ceilings that have been patched before. Two houses on the same street can differ by a lot on that alone.

Does the lead-safe rule apply to my house in Park Forest?

Probably, and the honest answer is that your build year decides it rather than the town. 90.2 percent of housing units in Park Forest went up before 1980, so most addresses here land on the pre-1978 side of the federal Renovation, Repair and Painting rule. It applies to work that disturbs paint, at roughly six square feet per room inside or twenty square feet outside, and to any window replacement. Check the year on your own address and ask whoever quotes you how they handle it.

My house in Park Forest is plaster, not drywall. Is that a problem?

It is not a problem, it is a different repair. Plaster cracks along the lath and comes back if it is only filled, so the fix has to address the movement rather than the line. With a 1958 median build year most of Park Forest is plaster over lath on at least some walls and ceilings. Say so when you call, because it changes the time estimate and it is better said before the quote than after.

Do you actually come out to Park Forest, or is this just a page?

It is 18.9 straight-line miles from the shop in Bridgeview, so it is a genuine drive and the answer depends on the job. A full exterior or a whole interior is worth the trip. One small patch on its own usually is not, and you will be told that rather than quoted a number that quietly covers the travel. Call 708-935-4289 and ask before you plan around it.
